title: EC-Council CEH
summary: The EC-Council Certified Ethical Hacker (CEH) is a vendor-specific, knowledge-based credential that certifies a practitioner can operate like an attacker inside an authorised engagement, using the same reconnaissance, enumeration and exploitation tooling as an adversary in order to find weaknesses before someone hostile does. It suits network and system administrators, SOC analysts, auditors, developers and career changers who need a working command of offensive tradecraft rather than a single toolchain, and it assumes reasonable grounding in networking, operating systems and defensive controls. To an employer the certification signals familiarity with a broad, structured methodology spanning network, web, wireless, mobile, cloud, IoT and operational technology targets, together with an understanding of authorisation, scope and the legal and ethical boundaries of testing. The knowledge exam is a proctored, primarily multiple-choice instrument drawn from a large item pool in a single timed sitting, with scenario items that ask the candidate to choose the appropriate technique, tool category or countermeasure, and the terminology of commercial tools appears throughout. EC-Council also offers a separate practical examination in which candidates work through challenge scenarios against live systems within a fixed window, and many candidates sit both. Because multiple-choice testing rewards recognition over recall, self-study alone tends to plateau; candidates who build isolated lab ranges, run the tools against deliberately vulnerable systems they own, and read the resulting packets and logs retain the material, recognise the phrasing used in items, and finish the sitting with time to spare.
objectives: Ethical and Legal Framework: covers authorisation, scope definition, rules of engagement, and the professional and legal limits placed on offensive testing.
Footprinting and Reconnaissance: covers passive and active information gathering against an authorised target, including open-source, DNS and infrastructure profiling.
Scanning and Enumeration: covers host discovery, port and service identification, and extracting account, share, service and directory detail from reachable systems.
Vulnerability Analysis: covers identifying and validating weaknesses, interpreting scanner output critically, and ranking issues by realistic business impact.
System Attack Techniques: covers password, privilege and access attacks against authorised hosts, including how small weaknesses are chained into a foothold.
Malware and Payload Concepts: covers how malicious software is categorised, delivered and controlled, and how defenders recognise it without handling live samples.
Sniffing, Session and Denial-of-Service Concepts: covers traffic interception, session handling weaknesses and resource-exhaustion attacks at a conceptual and defensive level.
Web, Database and Application Attacks: covers server and application weaknesses, injection classes, and the controls that reliably prevent them.
Wireless, Mobile, IoT and Operational Technology: covers the attack surface of radio, handheld, embedded and industrial environments and the controls specific to each.
Cloud and Container Attack Surface: covers identity, storage and configuration weaknesses in hosted environments and the shared-responsibility questions they raise.
Cryptography: covers encryption, hashing, PKI and common implementation mistakes, and how cryptography both protects a target and undermines it when misused.
Evasion and Defence Awareness: covers how attackers avoid detection and how firewalls, IDS and monitoring are tuned and evaded in practice.

beginner.definition: CEH stands for Certified Ethical Hacker. It is a knowledge-based certification that teaches how attackers think and work, so you can find weak points before a real criminal does. It covers networks, web, wireless, cloud and more. The exam is mostly multiple choice, and it stresses legal permission and agreed scope.
beginner.whyItMatters: Defenders who understand attacker methods spot problems sooner and fix them faster. CEH gives you a broad map of those methods, plus the tools and words used in the field. It also teaches the legal side, which matters a lot. Testing a system without written permission can end a career, even if your intentions were good.
howItWorks: You learn reconnaissance (quiet information gathering) from public sources before touching the target.
You study scanning and enumeration, which means finding live hosts, open ports and useful account details.
You learn how common attacks work against systems, web apps, wireless networks and cloud services.
You look at each attack from the defender side, noting the control that stops or detects it.
You cover cryptography, legal rules and reporting, so findings are useful and defensible.
The exam then tests all of it with mostly multiple-choice questions in one timed sitting.
beginner.example: Imagine a shop owner who hires a tester to check the alarms. The tester gets a signed letter, a time window and a list of doors. Outside that window, trying the same doors would be a crime. The tester walks the route a burglar would take, writes down every weak spot, and hands the list to the owner. The owner fixes the locks. The tester never takes anything and never returns without permission. CEH teaches that same mix of skill and boundaries.
takeaways: CEH teaches attacker methods so you can defend against them, not use them.
Written permission and a clear scope come before any testing.
Learn the tools, but also learn the control that stops each attack.
